title: Medtech stocks: how to analyze medical technology companies
description: Medtech stocks: moat in the gross margin, factory leverage, the MDR certification gate. How to read medtech companies — with the universe's own numbers.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Medtech stocks are shares in companies that develop and manufacture medical technology products — cardiac catheters, sterilizers, hearing aids, dental implants, single-use endoscopes. The business differs from pharmaceuticals in one decisive way: a medical technology product is sold and generates revenue at every procedure, treatment or installation, and consumables generate recurring revenue year after year. In AK1A's universe the healthcare branch carries 25 companies, eight of which are pure medical technology: Boston Scientific, CellaVision, Coloplast, Elekta, Getinge, Ambu, Straumann and Sonova. Between them lies the whole craft of medtech analysis: the gross margin moat, the factory's leverage and the regulatory gate. The healthcare branch is one of the universe's largest — and the branch that last received its own industry guide.

The guide walks through the mechanisms with the universe's own numbers (raw data 2026-09-03/17/18). As always: education in method, never advice about individual stocks.

## What are medtech stocks — products, not molecules

Pharmaceutical stocks are about molecules: a pipeline, phase I–III trials and a patent clock. Medical technology companies are about products: a finished good that is either CE-marked and sellable within the EEA — or not. This brings three differences to the analysis. First, revenues are procedure-bound: every operation, every hearing aid fitting, every wound care turnover generates a new sale. Second, consumables — Ambu's single-use endoscopes, Coloplast's intimate care products — create a revenue stream that behaves like a subscription business. Third, the moat is built on installed base and surgeon learning: the surgeon who has learned to operate with a particular stent system does not switch at the first opportunity. See the course [the moat concept](/kurser/mt-01-vad-ar-en-moat) for the anatomy of moats and [the healthcare sector](/kurser/km-048-halsovardsektorn) for the sector's basic structure.

One delimitation: the care providers Fresenius and Attendo sit in the same industry branch but are service companies — their costly staffing shows in gross margins around 25.4 and 36.9 percent respectively, against the product companies' above 60. Care provider analysis is a craft of its own; this guide focuses on the product side.

## The gross margin staircase — where the medtech moat shows

The universe's medical technology gross margins form a staircase: Sonova 73.7 percent, Straumann 69.3, Boston Scientific 69.2, CellaVision 68.7, Coloplast 67.2 — then a drop to Getinge 48.6 and Elekta 39.6. The span from the top to the care provider Fresenius is 73.7 − 25.4 = 48.3 percentage points. The staircase is no random value: it measures how much of the price the company keeps after manufacturing cost, and thereby who holds pricing power. The hearing aid goes through the audiologist who fits it; the implant is sold to the surgeon who has learned the system; the single-use product has documented function that the hospital cannot swap away on price. Larger hospital equipment — sterilizers, ventilators, operating tables — is instead often procured through tenders, and tenders squeeze the gross margin. CellaVision illustrates the mechanism from the other direction: the blood analysis instruments are installed at laboratories that then consume reagents and cassettes — the installation builds a revenue stream that follows sample volume, not new sales, a razor-and-blade mechanics of the same kind as print heads and coffee capsules. That is how the link between product type and staircase step works; the method is the same as in [gross margin analysis](/kurser/v07-bruttomarginal) and [the margin staircase and operating leverage](/kurser/ln-03-marginaltrappan-och-operativ-havstavng). The median of the eight product companies is 68.0 percent — a level few industries match.

## The leverage in the factory — Getinge's cautionary example

Medtech is manufacturing, and manufacturing has operating leverage: fixed costs stand still while volume moves. A worked example in the staircase's shape: a company with a 68 percent gross margin sells at 100 kronor per unit and has 32 kronor in variable cost — the contribution becomes 68 kronor. At a volume of 100 units revenue is 10,000, contribution 6,800 and, with fixed costs of 5,200, operating profit 1,600 (16 percent). If volume grows 10 percent the contribution becomes 68 × 110 = 7,480 and profit 2,280 — a profit increase of 42.5 percent, more than four times the volume increase. But leverage cuts both ways: if the price falls 5 percent on unchanged volume, revenue becomes 9,500, contribution 6,300 and profit 1,100 — 31 percent of the profit disappeared on a price change of one twentieth.

The universe's own example of the wrong side of the leverage is Getinge: between 2022 and 2025 revenues grew from 28,292 to 34,969 million kronor (+23.6 percent), but profit fell from 2,491 to 2,258 million (−9.4 percent). The net margin declined from 8.8 to 6.5 percent. Revenue thus grew into the factory without the surplus following — the cost base grew faster than sales. When you read a medtech company, the first question is therefore not how much revenue grows, but how much of the growth remains in the margin. Compare with [ROIC analysis](/kurser/roic-01-avkastning-pa-investerat-kapital): capital return per manufactured kronor reveals whether the factory is working right.

## The regulation — MDR, CE marking and FDA

Before a medical technology product may be sold within the EEA it requires CE marking under the EU's regulation on medical devices (MDR, 2017/745), which sorts products into risk classes I–III — from plasters to implants that support life. In Sweden the Medical Products Agency is the supervisory authority. In the US new products often go through the FDA's 510(k) track: the manufacturer shows that the product is substantially equivalent to an already approved one. The regulation is double-edged in the analysis. On one hand it is an entry barrier — a certified product library built over years is hard to copy, and re-certifications under new rulebooks postpone competitors' launches. On the other hand the same re-certifications can hit the company itself: a delayed certification freezes a launch while the factory's costs keep rolling. The method for weighing such degrees of regulatory exposure is covered in [regulatory analysis](/kurser/v18-regulatoriska).

## Valuing medtech stocks — quality is priced hard

Valuation across the universe's eight product companies spans widely. The median P/E is 30.0 (seven companies with positive earnings; Elekta lacks a comparable earnings multiple just there) and the median EV/EBIT 18.8. The P/E span runs from Boston Scientific 19.4 to Straumann 41.0 — more than double — and the EV/EBIT spectrum paints the same picture: Boston Scientific 17.1 against CellaVision 24.7 and Ambu 24.1, two different price tags on the staircase's upper steps. The ROIC median is 15.0 percent. The pattern is clear: Straumann, with a 69.3 gross margin and a 24.7 EBIT margin, trades at a clear premium; Elekta, with a 39.6 gross margin and a 10.5 EBIT margin — Straumann's EBIT margin is more than twice as high — trades on turnaround assumptions. It is the same logic as in [P/E analysis](/kurser/km-009-pe) and [the PEG multiple's weaknesses](/blogg/peg-multipeln-svagheter-2026): a multiple is a price on expected margin power, not a bargain figure. Companies with documented pricing power and consumable revenues command a premium; turnaround companies must show the margin development first — Ambu grew revenue 10.8 percent per year over five years with a gross margin of 60.1, and Sonova delivered 20.5 percent return on equity. [Return on equity](/blogg/v09-roe-analys) and the history of margins say more than single multiple figures.

## The checklist — five steps when you analyze medtech stocks

1. **Place the gross margin in the staircase.** Above 60 percent indicates pricing power; below 50 points toward tender competition. Compare with the company's own five-year history, not only with the industry.
2. **Calculate on the revenue structure.** How large a share is consumables and service (recurring) against one-off equipment sales (cyclical order book)? See [order book and pricing](/kurser/km-069-orderbok-och-prissattning).
3. **Follow the leverage backwards.** Divide the profit change by the revenue change — Getinge's example (revenue +23.6, profit −9.4) shows how a factory can swallow the growth.
4. **Check the certification status.** Which product families are MDR-approved, which await re-certification, and what exposure does the US FDA track carry?
5. **Price the margin, not the multiple.** A high P/E against a stable 70 percent gross margin and a low P/E against a falling 40 percent one mean two different risks — the span 19.4 to 41.0 in the universe is a spectrum of quality, not of price.

That is how a medtech analysis is built: the staircase first, the leverage next, the regulation as gate and the multiple as the price of everything else. For a deeper walkthrough of the sector methodology there is [the sector analysis method](/kurser/se-16-sektoranalysens-metod) and [the complete guide to Swedish stock analysis](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026).

_Sources: AK1A's 100-company universe (Yahoo Finance/MarketStack/StockAnalysis with S&P data, raw data 2026-09-03/17/18); EU regulation 2017/745 ([eur-lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/745/oj)); [the Swedish Medical Products Agency](https://www.lakemedelsverket.se); [FDA](https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices)._

_This is educational financial analysis, not investment advice._
